title: Global debt
subtitle: More than 300% of global GDP
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: Global debt has never been higher. Should we be worried about it, or is it a normal tool for financing growth and confronting crises?

hero.hook: Japan owes the equivalent of 260% of its GDP... and no one worries. Here's why.

blocks.text: Global debt, that of States, businesses and households combined, today exceeds **300% of global GDP**, an absolute record in economic history.

This impressive figure hides a more nuanced reality: debt makes it possible to finance growth, respond to health crises or prepare for the ecological transition. But it also carries with it the risk of a collapse of confidence.

sections.title: How a state gets into debt

blocks.text: A State goes into debt when its expenditure structurally exceeds its tax revenue. This budget deficit is filled by borrowing on the financial markets. According to , borrowing to stimulate the economy in times of crisis is legitimate, provided that it is repaid once growth returns. [[Keynesian theory]]

In practice, governments borrow easily in bad times, but rarely repay in good times. The debt then accumulates over the long term. The case of Japan is fascinating: with a debt close to 260% of its GDP, the country should logically be in crisis. However, it is not, because most of its debt is held by its own banks and savers, sheltered from foreign markets.
Only in 2015 did the United Kingdom finish repaying debts dating from the Napoleonic Wars and a financial bubble of 1720.
The real danger of a debt depends not only on its amount, but on the currency in which it is borrowed. Rich countries borrow in their own currencies, which reassures investors.

blocks.caption: Global public debt today exceeds 300% of the planet's GDP.

blocks.text: Developing countries often have to borrow in dollars, due to a lack of a currency considered stable enough. If their national currency loses value against the dollar, the amount to be repaid explodes overnight. In these crises, the  often intervenes, but generally imposes strict savings policies which weigh heavily on the populations. [[IMF]]

A debate opposes two visions of the economy.  asserts that a state cannot go bankrupt as long as it borrows in its own currency: the real limit is not an arbitrary figure, like the 60% imposed by the Maastricht Treaty in Europe, but the level of inflation. [[Modern Monetary Theory (MMT)]]

Other, more cautious economists fear that too much debt could scare away market confidence, leading to a sharp rise in interest rates. The eurozone crisis, between 2010 and 2012, illustrated this risk: countries like Greece, deprived of their own central bank, saw their borrowing rates soar to the point of threatening the very existence of the European currency.

Global debt does not only concern States: businesses and households also bear a growing share of it, sometimes via poorly regulated financial players. A new debate is also emerging around climate debt: should we treat the debt which finances the energy transition differently from that which finances simple consumption?

The question of justice between generations remains central: going into debt today means taking taxes from tomorrow. But if this money finances sustainable infrastructure or good education, it can also be seen as a gift passed on to future generations rather than a burden.

Global debt exceeds 300% of the planet's GDP, a historic record. Its dangerousness depends less on its amount than on the currency in which it is borrowed: Japan proves that a debt of 260% can remain stable if it is held locally.
